abstract: Gut microbiome (GM) flexibility extends the adaptive potential of host species in the face of rapid ecological change. Madagascar's endemic primates offer a powerful natural system to study GM plasticity as the island experiences substantial environmental change throughout the year. This is especially true in the eastern rainforests, which experience marked variation in temperature, rainfall, and fruit availability between the wet and dry seasons. To elucidate interactions between climate, diet, and the GM, we conducted a 10-month study of the ecologically flexible red-fronted brown lemur (Eulemur rufifrons) in Ranomafana National Park. We detected significant shifts in gut microbial communities correlated with monthly rainfall, temperature, and dietary diversity. Trade-offs between abundances of carbohydrate- and fiber-metabolizing bacteria reflected shifts between frugivory and folivory, suggesting that the GM buffers energetic and/or nutritional imbalances when resources are scarce. Finally, we observed synchronized shifts in climate and the GM despite deviation from normal seasonal patterns, demonstrating the GM's rapid response to environmental cues. Our results suggest that the GM contributes to phenotypic plasticity across seasons, enabling endangered primates to better cope with environmental stressors like climate change.
